lesson_title: The Bakkie and the Bag of Ore
hook_text: Two exports leave the same dock. One earns hundreds of rand. One earns hundreds of thousands. Same metal.
clip_script: Stand on the dock and watch two exports leave. First, a bag of iron ore: the country banks a few hundred rand and the wages of the digging — that is the whole story. Second, a bakkie: the country banks hundreds of thousands of rand, and folded inside that price are the wages of the furnace operator, the presser, the welder, the seat-stitcher, the electrician, the sprayer and the driver who delivered it — plus the profits and taxes of every firm along the chain. Same underlying metal. The difference is which country did the MAKING. Each making step — ore into steel, steel into parts, parts into bakkie — is adding value, and doing those steps at home before exporting is beneficiation. A country that only digs is selling the cheapest link of the chain and buying back the most expensive one, forever. And no factory stands alone: behind the plant queue the tyre, glass and wiring firms; in front stand the dealers and mechanics. Hundreds of businesses hang from one production line — lose the plant and a town loses an ecosystem.
visual_style: A split dock: a small sack of ore stamped with a tiny price tag sails one way while a bakkie rolls the other trailing a chain of glowing links — furnace, press, weld, stitch, spray — each link stamped with a wage; the chain then fans out into a web of supplier and dealer storefronts around one factory.
pacing: Slow reveal of the two price tags, accelerating through the chain of making steps, wide settle on the factory's web.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn who gets rich off the same rock — and how policy tries to change the answer.
